item.text: {"text":"Evidence supports testing objectives before expanding NextItNet’s architecture. [Wu et al., TOIS 2024](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf) show that sampled softmax emphasizes hard negatives and supports top-K ranking, but temperature matters: excessive sharpening lets a few difficult negatives dominate gradients. [Subbiah et al., 2024](https://research.google/pubs/improved-estimation-of-ranks-for-learning-item-recommenders-with-negative-sampling/) demonstrate sampled WARP/LambdaRank with corrected rank estimates, offering an alternative to pointwise training. These are transferable objective ideas, not demonstrated gains for NextItNet under this host protocol. Sampling-bias correction and false-negative correction address different problems; neither automatically solves the other.\n\nHardest-only mining deserves caution. [Adaptive Hardness Negative Sampling, AAAI 2024](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28709) reports that fixed hardness can create false-positive/false-negative problems and proposes adaptive hardness. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) finds substantial dataset-dependent accuracy/popularity tradeoffs across random, popularity, in-batch and adaptive sampling. Practical hypothesis: retain one NextItNet scorer/category; compare multi-negative sampled softmax against a separate moderate-hardness sampling variant, masking known training positives and tuning temperature/hard-negative proportion. Such masking removes known collisions, not unobserved future positives; adaptive hardness remains a heuristic for those. Compare objective/sampler changes separately from gating, using identical seeds, budgets and pinned macro validation HR@10. Larger training margins alone cannot establish validation improvement; these sources provide no direct evidence for gains on the four-category benchmark."}
